```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(Lab6)
library(microbenchmark)

suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 1000000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
```


## Lab Report 

### Brute Force Algorithm
### How much time does it takes to run the algorithm for n = 16 objects?
```{r}
microbenchmark(brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500))
```

### Dynamic Algorithm


### Greedy Algorithm 
### How much time does it takes to run the algorithm for n = 1000000 objects?
```{r}
microbenchmark(greedy_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:1000000, ], W = 5000))
```


### What performance gain could you get by trying to improving your code?

#### Brute force
The operations slowing down `brute_force_knapsack` are the `$` operator, the construction of the different subsets, and the `sum` operation. This could be improved by extracting the value and weight vectors once before the loop, and by vectorizing the subset evaluation, for example by representing all subsets as a binary matrix and computing all weights and values at once with matrix multiplication.

Such improvements would reduce the runtime by a constant factor. However, since the algorithm is $O(2^n)$, the runtime doubles with every additional item, so even a large constant-factor speed-up only allows a few more items within the same time. The algorithm is therefore not suitable for large $n$, and we have not implemented these improvements.

#### Greedy 
Initially, the greedy algorithm sorted the entire data frame and built the solution in a for loop, appending each selected item with `c()`. Profiling with `profvis` showed that this was highly inefficient: sorting the data frame was costly, and growing a vector with `c()` copies the whole vector on every iteration, giving $O(k^2)$ copying and frequent garbage collection.

After rewriting the algorithm to only compute the sorting order and to select items using vectorized operations (`cumsum`), we saw a substantial increase in performance. Using the built-in function `order()` also lets us use radix sort, which makes the sorting $O(n)$ instead of $O(n \log n)$. Since the rest of the algorithm is also linear, the whole algorithm now runs in $O(n)$ time.

#### Dynamic
One of the main contributors for the time and memory usage in the `knapsack_dynamic()` - function is the use of 
`max()` inside the `else{}` statment on lines 39-44. We instead perform a conditional check by replacing lines 40-42 with the code in 
the chunk below, the execution time decreases by approximatly 60\%. 
```{r, eval = FALSE}
without_item <- mat[i, capacity + 1]
 
with_item <- value[i] + mat[i, capacity - weight[i] + 1]
 
if (with_item > without_item) {
  mat[i + 1, capacity + 1] <- with_item
} else {
  mat[i + 1, capacity + 1] <- without_item
}
```

### Greedy RCpp
```{r}
x <- knapsack_objects

microbenchmark(
  slow = greedy_knapsack(x, W = 5000, fast = FALSE),
  fast = greedy_knapsack(x, W = 5000, fast = TRUE),
  times = 20
)
```

#### What performance gain could you get by using Rcpp and C++?
As we can see above, the "fast" Rcpp implementation is actually slower than the R implementation, at least for larger n. This is because the R implementation uses `order()`, which uses radix sort with a time complexity of $O(n)$, whereas the C++ sorting algorithm uses introsort, which is $O(n \log n)$.
The Rcpp implementation could be improved by also using radix sort, or by not sorting all elements at the beginning. If $W$ is much smaller than the total weight of all items, this could improve performance, since we usually do not need all items to fill the knapsack.
We have not focused on improving the Rcpp implementation due to lack of time, and because it is not the main focus of this course. 

#### A more "fair" comparison
Here we use shell sort in the `order()` function, this gives an _average_ complexity of $O(n \log n)$. 

```{r}
x <- knapsack_objects

microbenchmark(
  slow_shell = greedy_knapsack(x, W = 5000, fast = FALSE, method = "shell"),
  fast = greedy_knapsack(x, W = 5000, fast = TRUE),
  times = 20
)
```
